toc.title: How to use and not use the A->W->E method

blocks.p: You may have realized the safety anchors don't need to exist independently. Nothing is stopping you from using two or more of these Potentials simultaneously. In other words, you can stack or multiply these Anchoring Potentials to increase the likelihood of neurocepting a safety cue and anchoring into safety.

In fact, you will likely see some benefit from safety stacking active cues on top of the passive ones within your Passive Safety Environment. Like in the quote from Dr. Porges, "once the passive pathway effectively shifts our physiological state, the second step can be initiated," this applies to Safety Stacking. The passive cues activate the initial physiological safety state, and then you can take more active cueing steps, especially mindfully.

Your Passive Safety Environment serves as the foundation for stacking other Safety Potentials. Some anchors lend themselves well to this kind of layering. Movement anchors would probably stack well on top of musical anchors through dancing. Likewise, cognitive and musical anchors could stack on top of each other and the Passive Safety Environment through singing.

That being said, I'm unsure if you'll benefit from randomly stacking active safety Potentials on each other (I assume not). For example, if you were to taste a strawberry while reading, one of those two things would lose some of its impact. If you were to focus on the taste, the imaginative reading would suffer. If you were to focus on the imagination, then the taste would be less. Being mindful of an experience means focusing on one aspect of the experience at a time: either the taste or the narrative imaginary experience.

Of course, you will also need to be aware of the impact of safety stacking. There is probably a point of "too much" safety layering. There may be sensory overload, or your efforts may show diminishing benefits. As you add layers of safety, the impact of the others may lessen as well. If you feel it's too much, remove one of the stacks. I tend to do better with minimal and mindful safety experiences without stacking more and more on top of the experience. You may find yourself having a similar experience. Do what helps you to deepen your anchor into safety.

Perhaps the most beneficial stack you could add, and perhaps the most challenging, is receiving co-regulation. The passive and active safety cues and anchors can stack neatly with the presence of another who is providing co-regulation. Think of co-regulation as another passive safety stack. You don't need to do anything about it, except maybe be willing to receive it mindfully.

You can invite others into your Passive Safety Environment (including pets!). These others need to be capable of sending safety cues. That's two stacks of passive safety: co-regulation and the environment's passive safety cues. You can stack on an active safety cue or anchor, like yoga (movement), with a co-regulative other in a safety environment, creating a third stack. Or imagine doing some Q&A (cognitive) with them, or just listening to music, or remembering a moment you shared with them.

I know it's not easy. But it could be profoundly powerful in your safety stacking. If you can't get a person into your safety environment, meet them in another. And if that's not practical for you either, then hearing their voice on the phone might be helpful. Or seeing their face on a video call.
And if that's not realistic, then your pets are always a great option.
"Hey, Justin," you say, with a follow-up thought on your mind.
I respond with a curious, "Yes?"
"So I've set up my Passive Safety Environment and I love it. But what about the rest of my home? What about the outside world!?" You feel a slight panic.

Indeed! What of the outside world? You've created your safety environment, but what do you do now? Think of your Passive Safety Environment as your reliable place to go to practice being in safety. It's a constant stream of passive safety cues and the perfect place to try stacking other safety Anchoring Potentials.

And yet, the rest of your home and world do exist. And I don't believe you can take your Passive Safety Environment with you. (Although, at some point, we'll have glasses or contacts to do this for us in some way.)

Your vagal brake strength should increase as you practice being in safety and using your safety anchors. As it increases, the outside world should be more tolerable. That's the indirect benefit. However, I think there is a way to take more ownership over strengthening your vagal brake. And that would be through challenging your safety state.

What if you also practiced your safety anchors outside of your safety environment? The Passive Safety Environment is ideal for experimenting and identifying what works. Using these tried-and-true safety anchors outside the safety environment is great for reinforcing how well they work and increasing your distress tolerance.

At first, I recommend practicing inside and outside your Passive Safety Environment during your daily practices. Start inside, then do the same thing outside. And if needed, end by practicing inside of your Passive Safety Environment again.

This simple setup is a way to practice mild defensive activation outside of your Passive Safety Environment. Nothing should be wildly dysregulating, of course. But there is probably at least one space in your home in which you experience slight defensive activation, especially in comparison to your Passive Safety Environment.

The external environment that you pick to challenge yourself in should be manageable. A place you can succeed in with minimal challenge. As you gain mastery there, try another location. For example, practice in a spot in your home that is a little more noisy or cluttered. As that becomes easier, you could pick a more challenging spot, even outside the home.

Eventually, you can mindfully practice safety even in places that are not yours, like a doctor's waiting room or the DMV. Places like this are far less than ideal to practice safety. But eventually, you'll be able to practice safety cues here, too. No, I don't expect you to go there for this specific purpose. But while you're there for routine things, use these as opportunities to tolerably challenge your safety state.

But before then, practice safety Anchoring Potentials in your dedicated Passive Safety Environment. Then, challenge yourself in your home but outside of the Passive Safety Environment. As that becomes easier, challenge your safety state outside of your home.

The knowledge and practices you have implemented can reduce the intensity and frequency of your stuck defensive state activation. Strengthening your safety state is at the heart of these changes. When your safety state is stronger, defensive activation reduces. Eventually, you will be able to welcome defensive activation, even the stuck state resulting from prior traumatic incidents. That is where the A->W->E Method becomes useful.

I designed the A->W->E Method as a meditative practice blueprint to feel into your stuck defensive state and allow natural self-regulation to occur. It is a much more advanced practice, but we can lightly apply it here. Instead of feeling into your defensive activation, we can use the Method for feeling deeper into your safety activation.

Part of the reason you have remained stuck in your defensive "home away from home" is you lack an anchored capacity to experience your stuck state. If you are not anchored in safety, you won't experience defensive activation mindfully. If you don't mindfully experience defensive activation, your state stays stuck.

Once anchored in safety, you can direct your conscious awareness inward and more effectively access the experiences of your SSIEC domains, even the defensive ones. You can turn that awareness into witnessing the domains, which you can then develop into directly and consciously experiencing those domains. As you consciously experience your stuck defensive state, natural self-regulation can unfold.
These are the three steps of the A->W->E Method:

You know what being "anchored" is: accessing and maintaining access to your safety state. But after accessing safety, you can then mindfully direct your awareness toward it. Once focusing on your safety anchoring, you can then witness it.

"Witnessing" is acting as an observer, almost like an objective third party. Think of yourself as a curious researcher who is gathering data. This stance will help you extend your Anchored Awareness and Witness the safety state. You could Witness the general experience of what it's like to exist in your safety state through these questions:

ul: Where does safety live in my body right now?
On a scale of 0-10, how much safety do I have in my system?
Do I feel a general sense of connection?
Do I have access to my senses and the present moment?
Do I feel a sense of some type of goodness?
Do I feel a sense of like or dislike?

blocks.p: Just notice and take mental notes. If you can do that, you can begin to experience your safety state more deeply and directly.
If you can focus on the general sense of safety within you through Anchored Awareness and Witnessing, then the next step is to Experience being in safety directly.

Witnessing is a general overview. Experiencing is immersion. When Witnessing, you act like a commentator in a sports game. When Experiencing, you are on the field playing the sport. You do this by describing what it's like to be in your safety state. Instead of Witnessing it from afar, you Experience it through description.

Description can get very specific and detailed. For now, I recommend using simple descriptive options after you have identified where your experience is of safety within your body. After you have Witnessed its existence, ask yourself:

ul: Is there an emotion that comes with it?

blocks.p: Here is an example of how Experiencing sounds compared to Witnessing:

ul: Witnessing: "The safety state is active in my chest."
Experiencing: "The safety state is active in my chest. It feels warm, is a wavy yellow oval shape, and is comforting."

blocks.h: How to use and not use the A->W->E method

blocks.p: Let's return to a simple question: "What does connection feel like?" The A->W->E Method should give you a better understanding of what connection feels like. It helps you explore and experience your safety state.

You should not attempt to purposefully change anything through the A->W->E Method. The point is not to make your negative experiences go away, nor is the point to cause yourself to feel happy. Instead, the point is to immerse yourself in your safety anchoring more deeply.

The A->W->E Method can help you connect with your safety experience in the present moment. Allow an image of your safety state to come to your mind. Just be curious about it as it emerges and let more details unfold. You can also directly ask yourself those questions above.

I think there is a misconception about meditative practices: that they must be silent and devoid of cognitive words. My deepest, most meaningful meditative practices have combined all of my SSIEC, including words in my brain. The point is, don't be afraid to think while using the A->W->E Method.

You should not be using the A->W->E Method to feel into your defensive states at this point in your trauma recovery journey. I don't care if you've shared the trauma narrative a thousand times, or if you've cried innumerable tears, or if you've done all of the therapy modalities known to humanity. At this point, you should not be going further than focusing on safety and experiencing it through the A->W->E Method.

If safety is still relatively new, attempting to use the A->W->E Method might result in intolerable dysregulation. As we experience safety, defensive activation may come along with it. Your body attempts to self-regulate when it accesses safety, especially through the A->W->E Method.

However, at this point, you may not have the distress tolerance necessary for that. You can build your distress tolerance through continually accessing and exercising your safety state. Until then, deeper excursions into your safety state might not result in the safety that you want.

If you are ready for more challenge, one option is to use the A->W->E Method until you notice defensive activation. Give it a compassionate greeting when you see it, and permit yourself to end the meditative exercise. Once you end, recover and rest. If you can handle that well, repeat as you feel recovered and rested.

blocks.why: Anchored awareness, then witnessing: this practice is a gentle start, a few minutes at a time.

blocks.p: The defensive activation may become more tolerable over time, which is a good indication that your safety pathways are continuing to strengthen and allowing for more distress tolerance. Your safety state strength will become central to everything that comes next.
